4.5 — The Full State Machine: Patrol, Chase, Attack

You have written every line of this enemy already. Patrol. Chase. Contact damage. What you do not have is a place in the code that says which one the enemy is doing right now — and that missing field is the difference between a pile of behaviours and a machine. Today you name the states, draw the arrows, and choose how you want to represent them.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make an enemy switch between patrolling, chasing and attacking?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

The enemy should walk its beat, come for you when you get close, and hurt you when it reaches you — and on every single frame it should be doing exactly one of those three. "It behaves correctly, but nobody can say which one it is doing" is the whole problem.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Name the states this enemy can be inThree names — PATROL, CHASE, ATTACK — and nothing else. Written down once, in one type, so a fourth value cannot arrive by accident and the enemy cannot be two of them at once.Read: the Making states explicit section of the Enemy State Machines reference.
  2. write this partRead: the enum row in the Unity + C# Quick Reference, and the field-scope rule from 1.3 (the deadline you wrote as nextReportTime).
  3. Decide what moves it from one state to the nextOne assignment per arrow. state = EnemyState.Chase; is the transition — the comparison that used to decide whether to chase now only decides whether the machine becomes the chasing machine.Read: the four-part upgrade list in the Enemy State Machines reference, next to the transition table you drew at the top of this lesson.
  4. Keep the three behaviours you already wroteThe beat from 4.1, the pursuit vector from 4.3 and the contact damage from 4.4 are not rewritten. They move behind the state that owns them, and not one line of them changes.Read: your own EnemyController.cs after 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4 — the walkthrough below shows where each piece lands.

Three of those four parts are code you have already written, and the fourth is one field plus the line that reads it. That is the honest size of this lesson. What you have never had is a place in the file that says which behaviour is live — the state is implied by which branch happened to run, which is why you cannot print it, cannot drive an animator from it, and cannot answer "what is this enemy doing?" without reading the whole file.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the enemy switch between behaviours" cannot be looked up. "Declare an enum, hold one value of it, and switch on that value" can — and the reference page writes out all four pieces.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

The pieces table prices three ways to hold the states. Which did you choose, and what does your choice cost you — in your own words, not the table's?

ATTACK is entered by a physics callback rather than by a comparison. If you make it a real state, what changes about when the enemy moves — and is that the fight you designed in 4.4?

Your animator's Direction parameter is an Int with four values and no idle states. Now that the machine has a state you can read, what could you drive from it that you could not drive before?

In 4.1 your patrol ran on every frame, with nothing anywhere deciding that it should. What did the enemy store so it knew when to turn around — and is that a state, or a condition?

In 4.3 the chase hid inside an if, and the patrol was whatever ran when that if stopped matching. Which of the two could move the enemy while the other was also running — and what did the player see on screen?

In 4.4 the damage arrived from a physics callback, gated by a cooldown you first met in 3.3. Is ATTACK something the enemy is doing, or something that happens to it while it is doing something else — and which of those two did you actually write?

The turret in 3.1 fired the instant a distance check passed, and in 3.3 you gave it a memory so it could not fire every frame. What is the difference between a condition that is re-tested every frame and a state that lasts until something changes it?

The Problem: Where Is the State? ~20 min

Look at EnemyController.cs as it stands. Your patrol runs unconditionally, your chase hides inside an if, and your attack is a collision callback. The enemy behaves correctly — and yet there is no line anywhere that you could print to answer the question "what is this enemy doing?"

That is the problem. The state is not stored; it is implied by which branch of the code happened to run this frame. Before you fix it, draw the machine on paper — boxes for states, labelled arrows for transitions:

FromCondition or eventTo
PATROLdistance to the player is inside the aggro radiusCHASE
CHASEevery frame: move toward the player, normalizedCHASE (stay)
CHASEcontact with the player, and the damage cooldown has elapsedATTACK
ATTACKdamage delivered, cooldown startedCHASE
CHASEdistance is outside the radius (or outside the give-up radius if you built one)PATROL
One row of that table is a lie, and it is worth knowing why. In your code, ATTACK is not a state. It is a callback that fires whenever the enemy's collider meets the player's — which means it can fire while the enemy is chasing or while it is calmly patrolling. Walk into a guard on its beat and find out. Your diagram draws ATTACK as a state because that is how it feels to the player, and that is a legitimate reason to draw it. Just be able to say which rows your code actually implements.

Here are the ways to represent a machine like this. You are going to pick one:

RepresentationWhat it looks like in the fileWhat it buys youWhat it costs you
Implicit — the shape of the code is the state The chase is an if; the patrol is whatever runs when the if fails; the attack is a callback. No new fields at all, and the machine is short enough to read in one screen. This is what you have right now. Nothing can ask what the enemy is doing — not a Debug.Log, not the animator, not a behaviour you add in Unit 6. A third behaviour means nesting a third if, and the number of paths grows faster than you can read them. It also lets two behaviours run in one frame: the 4.3 bug, still in the file.
Boolean flags — one bool per behaviour isChasing, isAttacking, and one per behaviour after that. Cheap to add the first flag, and genuinely readable with exactly two behaviours. It is also the smallest change from what you have. Every flag doubles the number of combinations: four flags describe sixteen situations, and most of them are nonsense. Nothing in the language stops you from being "chasing and attacking and fleeing" at the same time — you simply get a bug instead of a compile error.
An enum state variable One enum listing the states, plus one field of that type, read by a switch. The set of legal states is written down in exactly one place, so illegal combinations cannot even be expressed. You can print the state name, drive the animator from it, and read every transition out of one switch. This is the version that survives Unit 8. One field, one enum declaration, and one transition rule — and you must decide every exit on purpose. The implicit version gave you the exits for free; here you have to write them down, and the one you forget is a state the enemy can never leave.
An enum, and one method per state The same enum and the same field, with each case in the switch reduced to a single call: case EnemyState.Chase: ChaseTick(distance); break; Each state's code becomes a named block you can read on its own, and the dispatch at the top of the frame reads as a table of contents. This is the arrangement that scales best when a machine gets big. You have to decide what each state is handed — the distance? the target? — and the transition now sits one hop away from the selection that reads the field. An extra hop, in exchange for a loop you can read at a glance.
These are not ranked — they are priced. Every row above is in shipped games, and the first one is what you already have. The question is never "which is correct", it is "which cost am I willing to pay for this enemy, this week" — and you have to answer it in one sentence you can defend to the person next to you. The implicit row is not an answer: it is the thing this lesson exists to replace.

Socratic: Naming the Machine

  1. Right now, is there any field in EnemyController.cs that holds what the enemy is currently doing? If not, what is holding it — and what does that cost you when you want to debug?
  2. With two behaviours, a single bool is perfectly readable. How many combinations do four booleans describe, and how many of those are real states? What does that ratio tell you about scaling the flag approach?
  3. Your attack is a callback, not a state. Can it fire while the enemy is patrolling? Walk into a patrolling enemy and find out — then say whether your diagram is a description of the code or a description of the player's experience.
  4. Your chase ends when the if stops matching. There is no "return to patrol" line in the file. Is an exit that exists as the absence of a match easier or harder to reason about than an explicit transition? Argue both sides.
  5. The AP exam names sequencing, selection and iteration as the building blocks of algorithms. Where is each one in your enemy? One of them is sneaky — think about what calls Update().
  6. If you print a state name every frame, what do you expect to see at exactly the boundary of the aggro radius? Which number would you change to calm it down, and what did you build in 4.3 that already fixes it?
Read the Docs: The Pieces of the Machine, in C# ~15 min

Whichever representation you picked above, it is assembled from the same pieces. Read all six rows — the last column is the one nobody reads, and it is the column that decides which arrangement suits your enemy.

PieceWhat it looks likeWhat it doesWhat it costs you
The enum declaration private enum EnemyState { Patrol, Chase, Attack } Declares the legal states once, as names the compiler knows. Nothing else in the file may invent a fourth one. It is a second list to keep in step with your diagram. Add a state here and the switch still compiles with no branch for it — nothing makes you handle every case, so a missing branch is silent rather than an error.
The state field private EnemyState state = EnemyState.Patrol; One variable holding which state is live right now. This is the thing 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4 never had. One more field to give a first value to, and its scope matters: declared inside Update() it forgets between frames. Leave the starting value off and it begins at 0 — whichever name you happened to list first, not the one you meant.
The selection switch (state), with one case per state Reads the field and runs exactly one branch this frame. The choice is now data, rather than the layout of your ifs. Exactly one branch runs, so anything two states genuinely share has to be lifted out of the cases or written twice — and the moment it is written twice, the copies drift apart.
The transition state = EnemyState.Chase; One assignment is one arrow: the comparison above it decides whether, the assignment decides where to. Every arrow has to be written by hand. The implicit version in 4.3 gave you the exits for free — the chase ended when its if stopped matching — so an exit you do not write is an exit the enemy never takes.
The break; break; at the end of a case Ends the case for this frame, so the machine runs one state and stops. It is easy to leave out, and there is no error message when you do: the machine falls through and runs the next case as well. The symptom is two behaviours in one frame, which reads as a movement bug rather than a selection bug.
One method per state case EnemyState.Chase: ChaseTick(distance); break; The case becomes a single call, and each state's code becomes a named block. The same machine, arranged differently. You decide what each state is handed, and the transition ends up one hop away from the selection that reads the field. A little more ceremony for a dispatch you can read at a glance.
Five facts a diagram of boxes and arrows cannot carry. The diagram shows you the shape; these five decide whether the machine in your file behaves like the one on your paper. Each is asked about again below.
  1. A machine can always say which phase it is in. That is what the field is for: the state has a name, the name can be printed, and a printed state is a bug report you can read off the Console.
  2. The type forbids a fourth state. Declare three names and three names exist — there is no fourth value to invent by accident, and no way to be in two of them at the same moment.
  3. A state can be real and still sit outside the loop. A vending machine carries an OutOfStock it may never come back from: reachable, legitimate, and not part of the cycle. Which transitions exist is decided by whoever wrote them, never by the type.
  4. The order is the behaviour. Warn, then lower, then wait, then raise — run those out of sequence and what you lost is the sequence. Some machines are a timeline wearing a state machine's clothes.
  5. A machine built from two booleans will eventually show both at once. In an enum that combination cannot be written down; in flags it is representable, which means someday it happens.

Each question below opens with one of those five facts, then asks what it means for your enemy. Answer from the table and the callout above, not from the player's script.

Predict Before Building

  1. Example 1 prints a phase name. What would the equivalent print look like in your current file — and what could you print today that comes closest?
  2. Example 2 says the type forbids a fourth state. Which illegal situation would your flag-based version allow but an enum would not?
  3. Example 4 says the order is the behaviour. Which part of your enemy is a sequence rather than a set of conditions — and what would break if the order changed?
  4. Example 5 says a two-bool signal will eventually show green and red together. Where in your own enemy could two of your bools disagree, and which one wins on that frame?
  5. Example 3 lists an OutOfStock state that is not really part of a cycle. Which state in your enemy is like that — reachable, but not part of the loop you drew?
Build It With MeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I make an enemy switch between patrolling, chasing and attacking?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs. Everything you built in 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4 stays: the beat, the pursuit, the contact damage and its cooldown. Today adds two lines to the class body and one selection inside Update() — the line that was never there. The names below are the ones this course uses; if you named yours differently, keep your names and read the shape.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Name the states, and give the class one field to hold the current one

Both lines go inside the class braces and outside every method — the placement rule from 1.3, and the reason an enemy can remember anything between frames at all.

    // ...the fields you wrote in 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4: speed, direction, the patrol memory, the aggro radius, the damage knob and its cooldown...

    private enum EnemyState { Patrol, Chase, Attack }

    private EnemyState state = EnemyState.Patrol;
  1. 1Not one of those fields is deleted or renamed today. The two lines below are the only additions to the class body.
  2. 3The legal states, written down in exactly one place. Three names, and from here on the compiler knows them.The type is the point. EnemyState.Patrol is the only spelling that compiles, so a typo is an error on the line you typed rather than a fourth state that silently matches nothing. A string holding "patrol" would compile happily — that is 4.2's lesson, where Direction meant Right on one controller and Up on the other and no error message ever mentioned it. private, because this is one enemy's own vocabulary and no other script has business naming its states.
  3. 5The field this whole lesson is about. One variable holding which of those three names the enemy is doing right now — the thing you could not print, could not drive an animator from, and could not ask about without reading the file.Two things to notice, and both are 1.3. Where it lives: in the class body, not inside Update(). Declared inside a method it would be rebuilt from nothing sixty times a second and carry nothing between frames — the same mistake as lastAttackTime in 3.3. What it starts at: Patrol. Frame one has to be some state, and a guard that spawns already hunting you has no first state at all; the beat you built in 4.1 is the machine at rest. Leave the starting value off and you get 0, which is whichever name you happened to list first rather than the one you meant.

Step 2Let the state decide which behaviour runs

This is the line that did not exist. Until today the patrol simply ran, and the chase ran if an if happened to match — two separate decisions, and nothing stopping both from being true in the same frame.

    void Update()
    {
        float distance = DistanceToPlayer();

        if (playerTransform == null)
        {
            state = EnemyState.Patrol;
        }

        ________ (________)
        {
            // one branch per state — the next step fills them in
        }
    }

    // No player is never in range, so the beat is never interrupted
    private float DistanceToPlayer()
    {
        if (playerTransform == null)
        {
            return float.MaxValue;
        }
        return Vector3.Distance(transform.position, playerTransform.position);
    }
  1. 1Still the every-frame method, and still where the enemy decides what to do.
  2. 3One measurement, made once, by a small method that answers the only question the machine ever asks about the player: how far away is it?This replaces the early return you wrote in 4.3. There, a missing player stopped the update dead. Here, no player simply means the machine falls back to PATROL — and the distance it is compared against is float.MaxValue, which is never inside any radius, so the beat can never be interrupted by a target that does not exist.
  3. 5The guard from 4.3, with a new job: it no longer stops the frame, it forces the state.
  4. 7An enemy with no target is a patrolling enemy. That is a state, not an exit — and it is the answer to what this machine does the moment your death rule from 2.2 takes the player out of the scene.An early return here would delete the machine. Return before the selection and no state is ever consulted again: the enemy freezes mid-beat, and the animator from 4.2 keeps playing the last clip it was given. The fallback for "no target" has to be a state, or the machine has a hole where its default should be.
  5. Your turn10The selection. Read the field from step 1 and choose which of the three behaviours runs this frame. One construct, three branches, exactly one of them running — this line is the machine.The multi-branch selection statement you met in 1.5: the one that reads a value and picks a branch to run. The value is the field you declared in step 1, and its type is the enum you wrote beside it.This is the line whose absence was the bug. Before today, behaviour was decided by where the code sat — the patrol ran because it was there, the chase ran if its if matched — so on any frame where both matched, both moved the transform. That is 4.3's two-writers bug, the hunter that crabs sideways because it is patroling and chasing at once. Now a value decides, the value can be printed, and there is no arrangement of this file in which two branches run in the same frame.
  6. 12The three branches land here. Nothing else in Update() changes: this selection replaces the unconditional patrol and the hidden chase, and the distance is still measured exactly once, above it.
  7. 14Closes Update().
  8. 16The small helper the line above calls. Two lines of body and one idea.
  9. 17A method with one job: return a number the machine can compare against a radius, whether or not there is anything to measure.
  10. 19The case that used to freeze the enemy in 4.3.
  11. 21A number so far outside every radius in the Inspector that no comparison in the machine can match it. "There is no player" is expressed as a distance, so the rest of the file never has to ask the question again.
  12. 23The measurement from 4.3, unchanged — the same two positions, the same call. If you chose sqrMagnitude there instead, keep it: what matters is that one place in the file answers this question.
  13. 24Closes the helper. One more } closes the class.

Step 3Move patrol and chase behind their states, and write both exits down

Every behaviour stays exactly as you wrote it — it only changes which lines it sits behind. What is new is the arrows: each state = ... line is one arrow from your diagram, in code.

            case EnemyState.Patrol:
                if (distance <= aggroRadius)
                {
                    state = EnemyState.Chase;
                    break;
                }

                // ...your beat from 4.1, unchanged: the anchor or waypoint check, the direction flip, the movement call and your animator line...
                break;

            case EnemyState.Chase:
                if (distance > aggroRadius)
                {
                    state = EnemyState.Patrol;
                    break;
                }

                // ...your pursuit from 4.3, unchanged: the normalized (player - me) vector, the movement call and your animator line...
                break;
  1. 1The state the machine starts in, and the one that runs when nothing is hunting you.
  2. 2The comparison from 4.3, measuring the same two things it always did. Its job changed: it no longer decides whether to chase this frame, it decides whether the machine becomes the chasing machine.The exit and the entry have to agree about the boundary. Your entry uses <=, so the chase's way out uses the other side of it — distance > aggroRadius. Use the same side in both places and an enemy standing exactly on the line changes state on every frame and stutters there instead of committing.
  3. 4The arrow. One assignment is the transition: the machine is now the chasing machine, and it stays that way until some line changes it back.One arrow, one assignment, and it lives in the case it leaves. If the chase code could also write state, two places would be deciding this machine's next move and which one won would depend on the order of the lines — the same class of bug as two writers on one transform in 4.3. A transition belongs with the state you are leaving, never with the state you are entering.
  4. 5Ends this case for this frame.The one line a switch has that an if/else chain does not. Leave it out and the machine falls through into the next case and runs the chase as well — in the same frame, from the state it was just leaving. Nothing crashes and nothing is underlined in red: the enemy simply behaves like two states at once, which is the exact thing this lesson exists to remove.
  5. 8The patrol itself is untouched. It now runs on the frames where the machine is in PATROL and on no others — which is the whole difference from 4.1, where it ran on every frame there was.
  6. 9Ends the PATROL case.
  7. 11The hunting state: entered from PATROL, and left by the two lines inside it.
  8. 12The return-to-patrol arrow, written down by hand. There was no such line in 4.3 — the chase ended when its if stopped matching, and the patrol was simply what was left. Now an exit nobody writes is an exit that does not exist.This is the line teams forget. Delete it and the enemy follows you across the entire map, forever, because nothing in the machine can leave CHASE. Notice also which radius it uses: if you built a second, larger give-up radius in 4.3, this is where it belongs, and the gap between chase-in and give-up is what stops the state flickering on the boundary.
  9. 14The arrow back to the beat. The beat resumes where it was — the anchor and the direction field are still holding the values 4.1 gave them, which is a decision you can make the other way if you want a fresh beat.
  10. 15Without it the machine falls through and runs the chase body on the same frame it decided to stop chasing.
  11. 18The chase body — the same subtraction order, the same .normalized, the same movement call. Nothing about the pursuit changes; it has just been given a state to live in.
  12. 19Ends the CHASE case.

Step 4Say what the machine does while it is attacking, and let physics enter it

ATTACK is the state your contact damage reaches — but not from a comparison. It arrives from the collision callback you wrote in 4.4, which is the only place in the file where the physics engine tells you the fight started.

            case EnemyState.Attack:
                if (Time.time >= lastDamageTime + damageCooldown)
                {
                    state = EnemyState.Chase;
                }
                break;
        }
    }

    private void OnCollisionStay2D(Collision2D collision)
    {
        if (!collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Player")) return;
        if (Time.time < lastDamageTime + damageCooldown) return;

        // ...the single damage call you wrote in 4.4, unchanged...
        lastDamageTime = Time.time;

        state = EnemyState.Attack;
    }
  1. 1The state a landing hit puts the machine into. Be honest about this one out loud: in your file the attack is not a movement — it is a callback — and this case is where you decide what the enemy does while a hit is landing. In this build that is nothing: no movement line runs here, so it stops for the length of its cooldown.Whether ATTACK is a state is a design decision, and this is where you make it. Your diagram draws ATTACK as a box because that is how the fight feels to the player; your code reaches it from physics, which means it can fire while the enemy is calmly patrolling. Both are defensible. What is not defensible is a state that nothing ever enters.
  2. 2The cooldown gate from 4.4 doing a second job. The same pair of fields that stopped the damage running every frame now says when the swing is over.The seed you chose in 4.4 matters here too. lastDamageTime is stamped the moment a hit lands, so this comparison is false for exactly one cooldown — and if you never seeded it in Start(), an enemy that has never hit you is already "finished attacking" on frame one.
  3. 4The exit: the swing is over, back to the hunt.
  4. 6Ends the ATTACK case. Every case in the selection ends this way, and every exit in the machine is a line you typed.
  5. 7Closes the selection.
  6. 8Closes Update(). One more } closes the class.
  7. 10Whichever callback you chose in 4.4 — OnCollisionStay2D, OnTriggerStay2D, or their Enter versions. The name is yours; the shape below is the same for all of them.
  8. 12The tag check from 4.4, unchanged — one extra hop through .gameObject for a Collision2D, direct for a Collider2D.
  9. 13The cooldown from 4.4, unchanged: a second touch inside the window is discarded, not queued.
  10. 15Your GetComponent call and the negative number you pass to the health method on PlayerController. Nothing about the damage itself changes today.
  11. 16The stamp from 4.4 that closes the damage gate. It is also the clock the ATTACK case reads to decide when the swing is over.
  12. 18The one new line here: the machine is now attacking. This is what makes ATTACK reachable — without it the state exists, compiles, and is never entered.This is the row of your diagram that your code does not implement the way you drew it. You drew an arrow from CHASE to ATTACK as if chasing led to attacking. In your file the arrow comes from physics instead: the enemy enters ATTACK from PATROL just as readily, which is why walking into a guard on its beat costs you health. Say that out loud once and you will never again mistake the diagram for the code.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • state declared inside Update() instead of in the class body

    You will seeThe enemy is stuck in one behaviour, or snaps back to PATROL on every frame, and walking in and out of the radius changes it only for an instant.

    Do thisDeclare it in the class body and only assign to it from inside a method. A variable declared inside a method is created fresh every time that method runs, so it cannot carry a state from one frame to the next. Same rule as lastAttackTime in 3.3.

  • a case left without its break;

    You will seeThe enemy chases and attacks in the same frame, and printing the state shows two names arriving in one frame. It reads as a movement bug, not as a selection bug.

    Do thisEvery case ends with break;. C# falls through to the next case otherwise — no error, no crash, just two behaviours in one frame, which is the bug this lesson exists to delete.

  • the state assigned in more than one place — the chase code also writes it

    You will seeThe enemy flickers between two states every frame, and which one wins changes when you move a line of code.

    Do thisOne arrow, one assignment, and every assignment sits inside the case it leaves. If two places can write state, you have two machines arguing over one field — the two-writers problem from 4.3, wearing a new hat.

  • the same side of the comparison used to enter and to leave a state

    You will seeStanding exactly on the aggro radius, the printed state alternates sixty times a second and the enemy stutters on the line instead of committing to a behaviour.

    Do thisEnter with distance <= aggroRadius and leave with distance > aggroRadius — opposite sides of the same boundary. If it still flickers in play, that is the signal to leave a gap: chase in at one radius, give up at a larger one. That gap is a number you choose, not an accident.

  • ATTACK left in the enum with nothing anywhere that enters it

    You will seeThe state name never prints in the Console, and the contact damage behaves exactly as it did in 4.4 — the state is decoration.

    Do thisSomething has to assign EnemyState.Attack, and in this enemy that something is the contact callback — the one place physics tells you a hit landed. A state nothing enters is a box on a diagram, not part of the machine.

  • the 4.3 early return kept in front of the machine

    You will seeDestroy the player and the enemy stands still forever — mid-beat, still animating, doing nothing. No state is ever consulted again.

    Do thisThe guard's job is now to force the state, not to stop the update: set state = EnemyState.Patrol; and let the selection run. "No target" is a fallback state, not an exit.

Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. This is the same machine arranged differently on purpose: the reference puts each state's code in its own method, so you can see that the arrangement was never the point — the state field, the selection that reads it, and the exits you wrote by hand are. Your names, your beat, your movement call and your damage flow are yours; the machine is what has to match.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class EnemyController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 2f;              // your number from 4.1
    [SerializeField] private float patrolDistance = 3f;         // the size of the beat (4.1)
    [SerializeField] private float aggroRadius = 5f;            // your number from 4.3
    [SerializeField] private int contactDamage = 1;             // your number from 4.4
    [SerializeField] private float damageCooldown = 0.75f;      // your number from 4.4

    private Vector3 spawnPoint;                 // 4.1 - the anchor, saved once in Start()
    private int direction = 1;                  // 4.1 - the sign that IS the beat
    private Transform playerTransform;          // 4.3 - however you acquired it
    private float lastDamageTime;               // 4.4 - the moment of the last hit

    // ---- all of today, in two lines: three names, and which one is live ----
    private enum EnemyState
    {
        Patrol,
        Chase,
        Attack
    }

    private EnemyState state = EnemyState.Patrol;   // frame one is a calm guard

    void Start()
    {
        spawnPoint = transform.position;
        playerTransform = GameObject.FindWithTag("Player").transform;   // or your wired reference
        lastDamageTime = -damageCooldown;           // "there has been no last hit"
    }

    private void Update()
    {
        // One measurement, and no early return: an enemy with no target is a
        // patrolling enemy, not an enemy that stops thinking.
        float distance = DistanceToPlayer();

        if (playerTransform == null)
        {
            state = EnemyState.Patrol;
        }

        switch (state)
        {
            case EnemyState.Patrol: PatrolTick(distance); break;
            case EnemyState.Chase:  ChaseTick(distance);  break;
            case EnemyState.Attack: AttackTick();         break;
        }
    }

    // Same machine, arranged differently: each state's code is its own method,
    // and the transition lives inside the method of the state it leaves.
    private float DistanceToPlayer()
    {
        if (playerTransform == null)
        {
            return float.MaxValue;                  // no player is never in range
        }
        return Vector3.Distance(transform.position, playerTransform.position);
    }

    private void PatrolTick(float distance)
    {
        if (distance <= aggroRadius)
        {
            state = EnemyState.Chase;
            return;
        }

        // ...your beat from 4.1, unchanged: the anchor check, the direction
        //    flip, the movement call and your SetInteger("Direction", ...)...
    }

    private void ChaseTick(float distance)
    {
        if (distance > aggroRadius)
        {
            state = EnemyState.Patrol;              // the exit nobody writes
            return;
        }

        // ...your pursuit from 4.3, unchanged: the normalized (player - me)
        //    vector, the movement call and your animator line...
    }

    private void AttackTick()
    {
        if (Time.time >= lastDamageTime + damageCooldown)
        {
            state = EnemyState.Chase;               // the swing is over
            return;
        }

        // Nothing here moves the enemy, so it stands still for the length of
        // its cooldown. If you would rather it kept coming, that is the one
        // line you move into this method - and it is a design decision.
    }

    private void OnCollisionStay2D(Collision2D collision)
    {
        if (!collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Player")) return;
        if (Time.time < lastDamageTime + damageCooldown) return;

        // ...the damage call you wrote in 4.4, unchanged...
        lastDamageTime = Time.time;

        state = EnemyState.Attack;      // physics is what enters ATTACK here
    }
}
Build Lab: Refactor to a Real Machine ~30 min

Open Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs — the file you built in 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4. The walkthrough above built the enum-and-switch row step by step. If that is the row you chose, you already have it working. If you chose boolean flags or one method per state, this is where you build yours: the five steps below are the same five for every row, and the answers look nothing alike.

Architectural specification for the state machine:

Step 1 — write the states down before you code.

  • What are the legal states of this enemy? Name them in capitals, and be honest about ATTACK: is it a state in your machine, or an event that fires while another state is active?
  • Which state does the machine start in, and what guarantees that on frame one?
  • What happens to the machine when the player is destroyed by your death rule from 2.2? Which state should an enemy with no target fall into, and where does the null guard sit relative to the machine?

Step 2 — choose the representation and refactor.

  • Enum with a switch, boolean flags, or an enum with one method per state? Pick the one you prefer and write one sentence justifying it against the others. (The implicit version is what you already have, so it cannot be your answer.)
  • If you chose the enum: what type holds the current state, what is its default value, and does it need to be serialized or private?
  • If you chose the flags: how many flags do you need for the states you named, and how many of the resulting combinations are real? Write the count down.
  • Whichever you chose: where is the state changed? Is it at the top of the frame before any behaviour runs, or inside each state's own code? What could go wrong if two transitions fire in the same frame?

Step 3 — dispatch the behaviour.

  • What does the top-level update method of the enemy now look like? Does it branch with a switch, an if/else chain, or one small method per state?
  • Where did your patrol code go? Your chase code? Your contact damage?
  • Which state is the default for a state you have not written a branch for — and what does the machine do if the value is somehow wrong?

Step 4 — the return to patrol.

  • Write the return-to-patrol transition down explicitly. What is the exact condition, and which of the two radii from 4.3 does it use?
  • When the machine returns to PATROL, does the enemy resume its old beat or start a fresh one? What does the player see in each case, and which does your code actually do?

Step 5 — prove it.

  • How do you print the current state's name so you can read it in the Console? With an enum this is nearly free — with flags, what do you have to write instead?
  • Which animator parameter from 4.2 could now be driven from the state directly, and where would that line go?

Save and play. Walk toward an enemy, let it catch you, then run away and watch the Console. You should see the state change in order — patrol, chase, attack, chase, patrol — as a sequence of names you chose.

Bug Hunt: Breaking the Machine

  1. Delete the transition back to PATROL. What does the enemy do after you escape? How is "no transition at all" different from "the wrong transition"?
  2. If you chose the enum, also add a bool isChasing and drive the chase from it. Now two sources of truth exist — where do they disagree, and which one wins?
  3. Set the aggro radius smaller than the distance at which the enemy can actually touch you. Can the machine ever reach your ATTACK state? Trace the arrows on your diagram to prove it.
  4. Remove the exit from ATTACK. What does the enemy do forever, and what would a game designer call that state?
  5. Print the state every frame and walk slowly across the boundary. Where does the printed state flicker, and which single number would you change to stop it?
  6. If you chose flags: add a FLEE flag. How many conditions are now nested in your update, and how do you know which one is in charge on any given frame?
Tinker ~15 min

Tinker: Design a Fourth State

  1. Invent FLEE: the enemy runs away when you get within 1.5 units. Which subtraction flips, what does the arrow on your diagram look like, and which state does it exit to?
  2. Invent ENRAGE: after being hurt, the enemy moves at double speed for three seconds. Which timing pattern from 3.3 do you borrow for the three seconds, and what new field does it need?
  3. Add a fourth state to your enum and count how many transitions you had to add. Now imagine the same thing with flags — how many did you save, and how many did you risk?
  4. Drive the animator's Attack trigger from the ATTACK state rather than from the contact callback. What changed about when the animation plays, and which ordering do you prefer?
  5. Commit and push: "4.5: explicit enemy state machine" — include a photo or an ASCII sketch of your diagram in the repository.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break "the enemy should switch between patrolling, chasing and attacking" into its parts before you write any code
  • Name, for each of those parts, the earlier lesson you lifted it from
  • Draw the enemy's state machine from memory, with a condition written on every arrow
  • Compare the implicit, flag-based and enum-based representations, and defend the one you chose
  • Say where the return-to-patrol transition lives in your code, and what condition it tests
  • Label sequencing, selection and iteration in real code
  • Explain why your drawn ATTACK state and your coded attack are not quite the same thing
  • Print the current state's name without a UI
  • Commit and push
